title: Letters and sounds
intro: Turkish is one of the easiest languages to read aloud, because it is written the way it sounds. This unit covers the 29 letters, how each one is pronounced, where the stress falls, and the big picture of how a Turkish sentence is built. Along the way you learn your first phrases: greetings, thanks and introductions.

blocks.text: Turkish has used the Latin alphabet since 1928 (the [interlude](a1-u01-culture) tells the story). It has 29 letters: 8 vowels and 21 consonants. There is no q, w or x; they appear only in foreign names.

blocks.title: If you speak French
blocks.text: Several letters match French sounds exactly: *ö* is the eu of “peu”, *ü* the u of “tu”, *ş* the ch of “chat”, *j* the j of “jour”, and *c* the dj of “djinn”.
English has one letter i; Turkish has two, and each has its own capital. Dotless *ı* goes with capital *I*, and dotted *i* with capital *İ*. The dot stays on the capital.

Writing “Istanbul” without the dot is a spelling mistake in Turkish: the city is *İstanbul*, and a sentence that starts with *iyi* starts with *İyi*. In the lessons, the keyboard bar under the answer box has *ı*, and *İ* with the shift key.

A circumflex (^) sits on a, i or u in a handful of loanwords. It is not a separate letter. It marks a long vowel, or a soft k, g or l before the vowel, and sometimes it is the only thing that tells two words apart: *hala* (aunt) and *hâlâ* (still), *kar* (snow) and *kâr* (profit). You'll also see it in *kâğıt* (paper) and *dükkân* (shop).

blocks.text: Turkish spelling is phonetic. Each letter stands for one sound, every letter is pronounced, and there are no letter pairs like English sh or ee. Once you know the 29 letters you can read any word aloud, even one you have never seen, and spell any word you hear.

items: Vowels are short and pure, with no glide at the end: *a* as in “father” but short, *e* as in “bed”, *o* as in “more” without the r, *u* as in “put”.
Two vowels side by side are two syllables: *saat* (hour) is *sa-at*.
Double consonants are held a little longer: *anne* (mother), *elli* (fifty), *teşekkür* (thanks).
*h* is always pronounced, even in the middle of a word: *merhaba*, *Ahmet*.
*r* is a light tap of the tongue, as in Spanish or Italian. At the end of a word it is often soft and slightly hissed: *bir* (one).
*v* is softer than in English, especially next to *o* and *u*: *tavuk* (chicken).

blocks.text: *ğ* is called *yumuşak ge* (soft g). It never starts a word and has no sound of its own. After a, ı, o or u it makes the vowel before it long: *dağ* (mountain) sounds like “daa”, *doğru* (true, right) like “dooru”. Between front vowels it can sound like a light y: *değil* (not) is close to “deyil”.

blocks.text: Most Turkish words are stressed on the **last** syllable: *kitap* (ki-TAP, book), *öğretmen* (öğ-ret-MEN, teacher), *teşekkürler* (te-şek-kür-LER). First names follow the rule too: *Ayşe* (ay-ŞE), *Mehmet* (meh-MET). Turkish stress is light: the stressed syllable is a little higher and stronger, not much louder.
When you add a suffix, the stress usually moves along to the new last syllable: *ev* (house) → *evler* (ev-LER, houses). A few suffixes never take the stress; you'll meet them in later units.

Stress rarely changes the meaning of a word, so don't let it slow you down. Copy the voice in the lessons and the exceptions will come with practice.

sections.title: How a Turkish sentence is built

blocks.text: Four features make Turkish quite different from English or French. You don't need to master them yet, but knowing them now will make each new unit easier to place.
**1. Suffixes stack on a root.** Turkish adds endings to a word, one after another, and each ending has one job. Where English uses separate words (my, in) or a plural s, Turkish uses a suffix:
**2. The verb comes last.** The usual order is subject, object, verb: *Elif çay içiyor* is literally “Elif tea is drinking”. You'll build sentences like this in [unit 6](a1-u06).
**3. No gender, and no word for the.** One word, *o*, means he, she and it. *Çay* can mean tea or the tea, and *bir* (one) doubles as a or an: *bir çay* (a tea).
**4. Pronouns are often dropped.** Endings already show who is speaking, so *ben* (I) and *sen* (you) are used mainly for emphasis or contrast.
The simplest sentences have no verb at all. To introduce yourself, put your name after *Benim adım* (my name) or after *ben* (I):

lines.tr: Merhaba! Benim adım Elif. Adın ne?
lines.en: Hello! My name is Elif. What's your name?

blocks.title: Learn phrases whole
blocks.text: *Benim adım*, *Adın ne?*, *Nasılsın?* and *Memnun oldum* contain grammar you will only meet in later units. For now, learn them as whole phrases; each one will make sense when its suffix comes up.

summary: Turkish has 29 letters. The new ones are *ç*, *ğ*, *ı*, *ö*, *ş* and *ü*; q, w and x are missing.
Each letter is one sound, and every letter is pronounced: read what you see, write what you hear.
*ı* and *i* are different letters with different capitals: *I* and *İ*.
*ğ* never starts a word; it lengthens the vowel before it.
Stress usually falls on the last syllable; most place names (*Ankara*) and some adverbs (*şimdi*) are exceptions.
Suffixes stack on a root, the verb comes last, and there is no gender and no word for **the**.
*Merhaba*, *Benim adım…*, *Memnun oldum*: fixed phrases are enough for a first conversation.
